dossiers.title: Behavioral sleep extension
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis found that behavioral sleep-extension interventions increased sleep duration versus control or baseline; direct sleep-schedule interventions had larger effects than indirect educational or coaching approaches.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Behavioral sleep-extension interventions increase sleep duration on average
dossiers.population: Studies included adults, college students, and children aged 12+; 19 enrolled adults
dossiers.applicability: Conditional support for adults in the target program with a stable 14+ night pattern of short total sleep or limited time in bed; supports creating more sleep opportunity, not a diagnosis or a promised health outcome
limitations: The review pooled heterogeneous populations, intervention components, and study designs; heterogeneity was high
Not every included study was an adult randomized trial, so the action must be phrased cautiously for adults
The review establishes sleep-duration change, not a guaranteed cardiometabolic, mood, or performance benefit
The wearable-only schema cannot identify why sleep opportunity is limited or whether a clinical sleep disorder is present

source.title: Behavioral interventions to extend sleep duration: A systematic review and meta-analysis
source.locator: Abstract/Results: 42 studies from 14 countries; two-arm pooled SMD 0.80 (95% CI 0.28-1.31); direct schedule interventions had larger effects

dossiers.title: Sleep regularity as a health dimension
dossiers.claim_summary: The AASM lists regularity alongside duration, timing, quality, and absence of sleep disorders as a constituent dimension of healthy sleep.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Regularity is framed as a necessary dimension of healthy sleep
dossiers.population: Public-health position statement; no single study population
dossiers.applicability: Supports treating regularity as a dimension worth reporting; does not license a quantified regularity target
limitations: No graded recommendation or numeric threshold for regularity
Does not establish that intervening on regularity improves outcomes

source.title: Sleep is essential to health: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine position statement
source.locator: INTRODUCTION: 'Healthy sleep requires adequate sleep duration, appropriate timing, regularity, the absence of sleep disorders, and good quality'

dossiers.title: Sleep regularity and mortality association
dossiers.claim_summary: Lower sleep regularity, measured by the accelerometer-derived Sleep Regularity Index, is associated with higher all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality risk.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Lower regularity is associated with higher mortality risk, non-linearly
dossiers.population: 88,975 UK Biobank participants, mean age 62 (SD 8), 56% female, 7.1-year mean follow-up
dossiers.applicability: Mean age 62 exceeds the 18-64 target range at the older end; extrapolation to younger adults must be stated as such
limitations: Observational design; authors state it is unclear whether interventions that improve regularity extend lifespan
Residual confounding cannot be excluded
Sleep-wake states inferred from accelerometry, with misclassification versus polysomnography
No sleep diaries; algorithm identified only the main sleep period and did not detect naps

source.title: Sleep regularity and mortality: a prospective analysis in the UK Biobank
source.locator: Figure 1 A/B/C adjusted hazard ratios; SRI 5th percentile all-cause HR 1.53 (95% CI 1.41-1.66)

dossiers.title: Reversible sleep-schedule consistency experiment
dossiers.claim_summary: A National Sleep Foundation expert panel reached formal consensus that daily regularity in sleep timing is important for health and performance, after reviewing 63 full-text publications. The statement supports a cautious schedule-consistency experiment, not a universal timing target or a claim that a weekday-weekend gap is a disorder.
dossiers.evidence_basis: More regular sleep timing is endorsed as an important component of sleep health and performance
dossiers.population: Adults; formal consensus informed by a systematic literature review and expert panel
dossiers.applicability: When repeated reportable weekday-weekend timing differences are present, supports one low-risk, reversible attempt to make wake times or the sleep window more consistent while observing the pattern. When weekdays are shorter and weekends are longer, preserving sleep opportunity takes priority over merely shrinking the timing gap. It does not establish social jetlag, circadian phase, a disease, or an individual outcome.
limitations: The underlying evidence is predominantly observational, so it does not establish the effect size of changing one person's schedule
The consensus does not provide a universal hour threshold, bedtime, wake time, or rate of adjustment
Calendar weekday versus weekend is only a proxy for workdays versus free days in the current data
The panel also considered weekend catch-up sleep relevant when sleep is insufficient on weekdays, so reducing weekend sleep is not an appropriate default response to every timing gap
A timing difference can reflect ordinary commitments and does not diagnose circadian misalignment
prohibited_uses: Do not label a calendar weekday-weekend difference as social jetlag or a circadian disorder
Do not claim that schedule regularization will improve health, sleep duration, sleep efficiency, alertness, or disease risk for this individual
Do not use this card when the observed weekday-weekend contrast is small or not reportable
Do not turn it into a generic sleep-hygiene checklist

source.title: The importance of sleep regularity: a consensus statement of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel
source.organization: National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel (Sletten et al.)
source.locator: Abstract/Results: 63 publications informed a modified Delphi RAND/UCLA consensus process; panel consensus addressed daily sleep-timing regularity and weekday/workday catch-up sleep

dossiers.title: Sleep timing and consistency context
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review found later sleep timing and greater sleep variability were generally associated with adverse health outcomes, with GRADE certainty ranging from very low to moderate.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Greater variability and later timing are associated with worse outcomes
dossiers.population: 41 articles, 92,340 adults aged 18+ across 14 countries, 14 health outcome categories
dossiers.applicability: Covers the target age range; evidence base is observational so wording must remain associational
limitations: Author-assessed GRADE certainty very low to moderate across designs and outcomes
Most studies reported linear associations, so no threshold for excessive variability can be defined
63% of included studies relied on self-reported sleep

source.title: Sleep timing, sleep consistency, and health in adults: a systematic review
source.organization: Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism (Chaput et al.)
source.locator: Abstract GRADE statement and Conclusion; PROSPERO CRD42019119534

dossiers.title: Limits of regularity evidence
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review of sleep variability and cardiometabolic health found predominantly null associations for social jetlag with BMI and insulin resistance, and inconsistent cardiovascular results.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Null or inconsistent for several cardiometabolic outcomes
dossiers.population: 63 studies of adult and mixed populations with cardiometabolic outcomes
dossiers.applicability: Boundary for regularity interpretation: effects depend heavily on the regularity index and outcome, so do not present any regularity association as universal or settled
limitations: Authors describe findings across outcomes as mixed and inconsistent
Different regularity metrics yield divergent conclusions, so metric choice materially changes the result

source.title: Associations between sleep variability and cardiometabolic health: A systematic review
source.organization: Sleep Medicine Reviews (Zhu, Reutrakul et al.)
source.locator: Abstract Results: 13 social-jetlag studies (n=30,519) with nine reporting a null association; insulin resistance null across 5 studies (n=6,416)

dossiers.title: Sleep midpoint is not a precise circadian-phase measure
dossiers.claim_summary: Sleep midpoint is the behavioural marker most strongly related to dim light melatonin onset, but 7-day diary or actigraphy midpoint models still show limits of agreement of about plus or minus 1.8 to 1.9 hours, so no method estimates circadian phase precisely.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Constrains interpretation; individual-level precision is insufficient
dossiers.population: 72 healthy adults (36 female, 36 male), mean age 23.1 (SD 3.6)
dossiers.applicability: Caps how sleep midpoint may be interpreted: usable as a group-level phase proxy, not as an individual circadian measurement
limitations: Authors conclude no method is precise; fixed-interval methods carry proportional bias
Sample is young healthy adults around age 23, not the full 18-64 range
Single DLMO reference measurement
Authors state suitability is limited to research purposes, not individual clinical interpretation

source.title: Finding DLMO: estimating dim light melatonin onset from sleep markers derived from questionnaires, diaries and actigraphy
source.locator: Abstract Results and Conclusion: 'none of the methods provided precise estimates of DLMO'

dossiers.title: Consumer sleep-stage accuracy limits
dossiers.claim_summary: Across six consumer wrist wearables, four-state epoch-by-epoch agreement with polysomnography was only fair to moderate (Cohen's kappa 0.21-0.53; Fitbit Sense 0.42, Charge 5 0.41), and wake specificity ranged from 29 to 52 percent.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Unfavourable to stage-level accuracy; wake and light sleep worst
dossiers.population: 62 adults (52 male, 10 female), mean age 46.0 (SD 12.6), single laboratory night, recruited from a sleep-centre population
dossiers.applicability: Governs how far any stage metric may be interpreted; sleep-centre sample limits generalization to healthy community adults
limitations: Validation limited to the 8-hour lights-out window, restricting real-world generalizability
Single night with no multi-night adaptation
Proprietary algorithms are updated periodically, undermining cross-study comparability
Narrow age range and marked sex imbalance (52 male, 10 female)

source.title: A performance validation of six commercial wrist-worn wearable sleep-tracking devices for sleep stage scoring compared to polysomnography
source.organization: Sleep Research Society (SLEEP Advances), University of Antwerp
source.locator: Results 'Sleep stages' Tables 8-11; Methods 'Epoch-by-epoch analysis'

dossiers.title: Sleep-stage error may scale with stage duration
dossiers.claim_summary: Consumer stage estimation error is proportional rather than constant: devices overestimated shorter light and deep sleep and underestimated longer light and deep sleep, and overestimated short wake times while underestimating long ones.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Magnitude-dependent bias in stage and wake estimates
dossiers.population: 53 healthy adults aged 18-30 (31 female, 22 male), screened to exclude cardiac, neurological, psychological, and sleep disorders; one laboratory night
dossiers.applicability: Means stage errors do not cancel out and cannot be corrected with a fixed offset; sample is 18-30, narrower than the 18-64 target
limitations: Single night, so night-to-night variability is unaccounted for
Sample not racially diverse, and PPG is less accurate in darker skin tones
All devices experienced software, sync, or fit failures
Past device upgrades did not improve sensitivity or specificity

source.title: Evaluating Accuracy in Five Commercial Sleep-Tracking Devices Compared to Research-Grade Actigraphy and Polysomnography
source.locator: Results 3.5 'Light Sleep', 3.6 'Deep Sleep', 3.7 'REM Sleep'; Section 5 'Limitations'

dossiers.title: Sleep stages vary between people
dossiers.claim_summary: Stable trait-like inter-individual differences were found for 17 of 18 polysomnographic sleep variables (intraclass correlations 36-89 percent, highest for slow-wave sleep and NREM delta power), exceeding the group-average effect of 36 hours of sleep deprivation.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports person-specific rather than population-target interpretation
dossiers.population: 21 screened healthy young adults, 8 laboratory nights with blind scoring
dossiers.applicability: Supports interpreting stage architecture as person-specific; forbids comparing an individual against population stage percentages as a target
limitations: Any independent functional significance of these sleep phenotypes remains undetermined
Small sample of young adults in a highly controlled laboratory setting
Sleep variables were not fully independent of one another

source.title: Trait interindividual differences in the sleep physiology of healthy young adults
source.locator: Abstract Results: ICC range and slow-wave sleep versus 36-hour sleep-deprivation comparison

dossiers.title: Sleep stages vary from night to night
dossiers.claim_summary: Across 470 home nights, night-to-night coefficient of variation was high (0.44-0.58) for N2, N3, sleep latencies, and wake after sleep onset, and low (0.04-0.19) for sleep efficiency, total sleep time, and REM percentage, indicating single-night stage values are unreliable.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports multi-night aggregation over single-night interpretation
dossiers.population: 94 males self-reporting absence of sleep disorders, five consecutive weeknights at home with a headband EEG monitor
dossiers.applicability: Justifies aggregating over multiple nights and argues against acting on any single night; male-only sample limits sex generalizability
limitations: Authors note night-to-night variability is generally underestimated and under-recognized
Measured by portable headband EEG rather than laboratory polysomnography
Weeknights only
Male-only sample, so sex generalizability is unaddressed

source.title: Objective multi-night sleep monitoring at home: variability of sleep parameters between nights and implications for the reliability of sleep assessment in clinical trials
source.locator: Abstract Results: coefficient-of-variation tiers and minimum nights estimates

dossiers.title: Minimum nights for habitual sleep estimates
dossiers.claim_summary: In 107,144 Fitbit nights from 1,041 working adults aged 21-40 years, 3-5 nights produced good to very-good weekly mean total-sleep estimates, whereas 5-10 nights were needed for monthly estimates; estimating variability required longer observation than estimating a mean.
dossiers.evidence_basis: More nights improve reliability of habitual consumer-tracker sleep estimates, especially for variability
dossiers.population: 1,041 working adults aged 21-40 years using Fitbit in Singapore
dossiers.applicability: Supports treating multi-night aggregation as more stable than a single night and supports the runtime's distinction between short observation windows, stable levels, and higher-bar change/variability claims.
limitations: Working adults aged 21-40 in one setting; transfer to older adults and other populations is uncertain
The results concern reliability of aggregated estimates, not a health threshold or an intervention effect
The study cannot determine whether a change in one person's wearable estimate represents a clinical change
Weekly and monthly windows should not be conflated with the current non-overlapping earlier-recent comparison

source.title: Minimum number of nights for reliable estimation of habitual sleep using a consumer sleep tracker
source.locator: Abstract: 107,144 nights, 1,041 working adults aged 21-40; ICC thresholds for weekly and monthly total sleep time and variability

dossiers.title: Window length affects regularity estimates
dossiers.claim_summary: In a 14-day actigraphy study of 41 people undergoing sleep-disorder evaluation, regularity and fragmentation estimates based on fewer than 7 full days showed greater bias and wider agreement limits; the authors recommend at least 7 full days for these measures.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Longer observation windows reduce error in regularity and fragmentation estimates
dossiers.population: 41 people undergoing clinical sleep-disorder evaluation with 14 days of actigraphy
dossiers.applicability: Supports the runtime's rule that shorter than 7 days should not be used for stable regularity or fragmentation claims, and that a two-window comparison needs at least 7 nights per window.
limitations: Small clinically referred sample, not a general consumer-wearable cohort
Examined non-parametric actigraphy rhythm measures rather than this project's exact weekday-weekend contrasts
Does not establish a health threshold, diagnosis, or action
The current consumer source differs from research actigraphy

source.title: How many days are enough? Sleep-wake timing regularity and fragmentation scores change with the number of days included
source.organization: Journal of Sleep Research (Lok et al.)
source.locator: Abstract: 14-day actigraphy comparison; fewer than 7 days increased bias/variance; minimum 7 full days recommended

dossiers.title: Time-in-bed field semantics
dossiers.claim_summary: Fitbit defines timeInBed as total minutes in bed and minutesAwake as accumulated wake minutes excluding time before sleep onset and after final awakening, and states the efficiency value returned for stages logs should be ignored.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Not applicable
dossiers.population: Not applicable; device field definition
dossiers.applicability: Engineering semantics only; establishes that these fields carry conditional reliability and must not ground a sleep-medicine conclusion
limitations: The efficiency field is valid only for classic logs; using it for stages logs produces systematic error
Wake periods of three minutes or less are placed in shortData rather than data, so aggregation conventions must be unified explicitly
infoCode may signal insufficient heart-rate data or a period under three hours, so data quality is not constant
Mid-sleep wake over one hour splits a log while gaps under one hour may be stitched, affecting cross-day aggregation
dateOfSleep is the wake date rather than the sleep-onset date
Legacy Web API scheduled for deprecation in September 2026

source.title: Get Sleep Log by Date (Fitbit Web API Reference)
source.locator: Response Description table (timeInBed, minutesAwake, minutesAsleep, infoCode) and Additional Information 'Sleep Efficiency Calculation'

dossiers.title: Wearable wake-detection limits
dossiers.claim_summary: In laboratory polysomnography comparison, a consumer wrist device detected sleep with high sensitivity (0.96) but detected wake with specificity of only 0.61, while overestimating light sleep and underestimating deep sleep.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Devices underestimate wake and overestimate sleep
dossiers.population: 44 healthy adults aged 19-61 (26 female), screened to exclude psychiatric and medical conditions
dossiers.applicability: Covers the target age range; establishes that wake-derived fields carry systematic error
limitations: Study was funded by Fitbit, Inc.
Single laboratory night rather than multi-night home use
Device model is Charge 2, no longer current, and algorithms have since been updated
Low wake specificity implies systematic error in recorded awake minutes
Authors state further validation is needed in other populations and settings

source.title: A validation study of Fitbit Charge 2 compared with polysomnography in adults
source.organization: Chronobiology International; SRI International Human Sleep Research Laboratory
source.locator: Abstract Results: sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.61; N1+N2 overestimated 34 min; N3 underestimated 24 min

dossiers.title: Sleep-efficiency denominator
dossiers.claim_summary: A methodological review in the AASM journal argues that using time in bed as the sleep efficiency denominator is conceptually problematic because time in bed includes non-sleep activity before onset and after final awakening.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Not applicable
dossiers.population: Not applicable; methodological discussion oriented to insomnia research and practice
dossiers.applicability: Establishes that sleep efficiency values are not comparable across sources, including between device output and research definitions
limitations: Methodological commentary rather than empirical research, and not an official AASM recommendation
Discussion context is insomnia research and clinical practice, limiting applicability to the target population
The proposed denominator requires diary items that wearable data cannot supply
Conflicts with the Fitbit definition, showing sleep efficiency is not directly comparable across sources

source.title: Measuring Sleep Efficiency: What Should the Denominator Be?
source.organization: Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine (American Academy of Sleep Medicine)
source.locator: Abstract; proposes sleep efficiency = total sleep time divided by duration of sleep episode

dossiers.title: Clinical boundary for insomnia treatment
dossiers.claim_summary: The AASM clinical practice guideline recommends multicomponent cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia in adults with chronic insomnia disorder, a diagnosed clinical population distinct from adults without a sleep-disorder diagnosis.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports referral rather than self-directed restriction of time in bed
dossiers.population: Adults with diagnosed chronic insomnia disorder
dossiers.applicability: Hard boundary: the guideline population does not overlap the target population of adults without a sleep-disorder diagnosis, so it may only support referral language and never a sleep-restriction directive
limitations: Guideline population is adults with diagnosed chronic insomnia disorder, which does not overlap the target population
Sleep restriction therapy is only a CONDITIONAL recommendation requiring clinical judgment
Addressed to clinicians selecting therapy, not to self-help or consumer device contexts
Sleep restriction carries risks such as daytime sleepiness and requires professional supervision
Guideline does not evaluate wearable-estimated time in bed as a trigger condition

source.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
source.locator: Recommendation 1 (multicomponent CBT-I, STRONG); Recommendation 4 (sleep restriction therapy, CONDITIONAL)

dossiers.title: Regular movement and sleep quality
dossiers.claim_summary: Across 81 randomized controlled trials in non-athlete adults, exercise interventions improved self-reported sleep quality and, in a smaller objective evidence base, sleep efficiency versus control; the review does not establish a wearable activity-minute, Active Zone Minute, or heart-rate-zone dose for any individual.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Regular exercise interventions can improve self-reported sleep quality on average
dossiers.population: Non-athlete adults represented across 81 randomized controlled trials; intervention types and baseline sleep concerns varied
dossiers.applicability: Conditional support for an adult who wants to test a sustainable regular movement routine as one possible sleep-supportive behavior; it is not triggered by a low step count or a heart-rate-zone total alone
limitations: The primary outcome was self-reported sleep quality, not a Fitbit sleep endpoint
Exercise type, duration, frequency, baseline health, and sleep concerns varied across trials
The review does not identify a safe or effective dose from daily Fitbit activity minutes, Active Zone Minutes, or HR zones
A daily activity-sleep association in this dataset cannot establish that activity caused that night's sleep pattern
prohibited_uses: Do not prescribe a numeric exercise dose from Fitbit activity fields
Do not claim that low activity caused poor sleep
Do not use HR-zone values as cardiovascular screening or a sleep-treatment target

source.title: Effects of exercise on sleep quality in the general population: A systematic review and meta-analysis
source.locator: Abstract: 81 randomized controlled trials, 6,193 participants; pooled PSQI and sleep-efficiency outcomes

dossiers.title: Schedule regularization and daytime sleepiness
dossiers.claim_summary: One prospective study in college students without sleep deprivation found that a regular sleep-wake schedule was associated with less self-reported daytime sleepiness; this preliminary result does not establish a general-adult intervention effect or a universal timing target.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Schedule regularization was associated with less reported sleepiness in the study population
dossiers.population: College undergraduate students without nocturnal sleep deprivation
dossiers.applicability: Background for describing persistent timing variability as a pattern worth considering; this single, student-based study is not mature enough to authorize a current wearable-only behavior recommendation by itself
limitations: Single older study in college students; not representative of the full adult dataset
Outcome was daytime sleepiness, not consumer wearable sleep metrics
It does not identify why timing varies or establish a clinical circadian diagnosis
The current data do not capture work schedules, travel, caregiving, or other constraints
prohibited_uses: Do not use this study alone to generate a schedule-regularization action
Do not diagnose delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
Do not prescribe timed light, melatonin, or sleep restriction
Do not use timing variability to infer alcohol, anxiety, shift work, or lifestyle choices

source.title: The effects of regularizing sleep-wake schedules on daytime sleepiness
source.locator: Abstract conclusion

dossiers.title: Alcohol timing as a conditional continuity check
dossiers.claim_summary: NHLBI guidance explains that alcohol close to bedtime may make sleep lighter and make nighttime waking more likely. It can support one conditional alcohol-timing option when repeated sleep-continuity disruption is present, but cannot show whether any individual drank alcohol or whether alcohol caused the pattern.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Alcohol close to bedtime may contribute to lighter, more interrupted sleep
dossiers.population: Adults seeking general sleep-health guidance
dossiers.applicability: Only for a repeated recorded-awake or fragmentation pattern that remains partly unexplained, and only as an explicit if-then option about alcohol close to the sleep period. The current data contain no alcohol exposure, so the text must not claim use or causation.
limitations: Alcohol exposure, dose, and timing are not present in the project data
NHLBI guidance is general health guidance rather than an individual intervention trial
Recorded awake minutes depend on sleep-wake classification and are not clinical proof of fragmentation
prohibited_uses: Do not state or imply that the reader drank alcohol
Do not give an alcohol option unless it begins with an explicit if–then condition
Do not infer alcohol exposure from recorded awake time or sleep stages
Do not invent a universal dose, serving limit, or number of hours before bed

source.title: Insomnia: Treatment
source.organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
source.locator: Healthy sleep habits: alcohol close to bedtime can produce lighter sleep and make nighttime waking more likely

dossiers.title: Evening exercise and sleep context
dossiers.claim_summary: A meta-analysis in healthy adults found that evening exercise generally did not worsen subsequent sleep, although vigorous exercise ending within one hour of bedtime might impair some sleep measures; it does not identify the timing of an individual's activity from daily summaries.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Evening exercise is not uniformly harmful to sleep; timing and relative intensity may matter
dossiers.population: Healthy adult participants in acute exercise studies
dossiers.applicability: May support a conditional statement that exercise timing could be considered when sleep changes occur; daily Fitbit activity summaries do not reveal exercise timing, modality, thermal stress, or proximity to bedtime
limitations: Most evidence concerns healthy adults and acute sessions
Findings for vigorous activity near bedtime were based on limited moderator evidence
The present daily activity data have no time-of-day information
prohibited_uses: Do not infer late exercise from daily totals
Do not advise avoiding all evening exercise
Do not prescribe activity timing from a single-night sleep change

source.title: Effects of Evening Exercise on Sleep in Healthy Participants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
source.locator: Abstract conclusion and moderator analysis

dossiers.title: Long-term wearable sleep patterns and health
dossiers.claim_summary: In long-term Fitbit data linked to electronic health records, greater sleep irregularity was associated with incident obesity, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, and average sleep duration showed J-shaped associations with several outcomes; this is not an individual diagnostic or intervention result.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Persistent sleep duration and regularity patterns were associated with several chronic health outcomes
dossiers.population: 6,785 All of Us adults with at least six months of Fitbit data and linked EHRs; median follow-up 4.5 years
dossiers.applicability: Background for cautious long-term-health framing of persistent duration or regularity patterns; never a personal risk estimate, disease hypothesis, or treatment indication
limitations: Observational design with possible residual confounding and reverse causation
Current cases have far shorter observation windows and no linked EHR outcomes
The study cannot determine whether changing one person's wearable sleep pattern changes disease risk
Fitbit stage associations may reflect heart-rate algorithm effects or occult health conditions
prohibited_uses: Do not name a disease as likely or present in the reader
Do not calculate an individual disease risk
Do not use sleep stages to infer atrial fibrillation or cardiovascular disease
Do not make an intervention promise about disease prevention

source.title: Sleep patterns and risk of chronic disease as measured by long-term monitoring with commercial wearable devices in the All of Us Research Program
source.organization: Nature Medicine (Zheng, Annis, Master et al.)
source.locator: Abstract; Fig. 4; Discussion and limitations

dossiers.title: Consumer trackers cannot diagnose sleep disorders
dossiers.claim_summary: The AASM states that given the lack of validation against polysomnography and lack of FDA clearance, consumer sleep technology cannot be used for the diagnosis or treatment of sleep disorders.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Restrictive for diagnostic use; permissive for engagement and self-tracking context
dossiers.population: Not applicable; position statement on United States clinical practice
dossiers.applicability: Global constraint on the whole pipeline: no output may take a diagnostic or treatment form
limitations: Statement identifies unmet needs including future validation, access to raw data and algorithms, and FDA oversight
Published 2018 and predates current-generation algorithms
Verified via Europe PMC metadata; publisher sites blocked automated access, so no finer locator was obtained

source.title: Consumer Sleep Technology: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Position Statement
source.locator: Position statement paragraph beginning 'Given the lack of validation and United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance'

dossiers.title: Free-living sleep extension
dossiers.claim_summary: In a four-week free-living study of healthy young adults who habitually slept under 6.5 hours, an individualized sleep-extension program increased actigraphy-measured total sleep time by about 47 minutes on average; it was a small uncontrolled study and does not establish an individual dose or clinical benefit.
dossiers.evidence_basis: An individualized increase in sleep opportunity increased actigraphy-measured total sleep time on average in the study population
dossiers.population: 30 healthy adults aged 18–35 with habitual sleep under 6.5 hours and no diagnosed sleep disorder; substantial screening exclusions
dossiers.applicability: Supplementary direct evidence for a cautious, feasible sleep-opportunity experiment when a 14+ night pattern shows short total sleep; it reinforces monitoring total sleep time and time in bed rather than prescribing a fixed bedtime
limitations: Single-arm study with 30 participants and no control group
Participants were young, healthy, screened adults, so transfer beyond this group is uncertain
The intervention included individualized discussion and adherence support that are not present in the current system
The result does not identify why a current case has short sleep or guarantee daytime, health, or clinical benefit
prohibited_uses: Do not infer that short time in bed proves limited sleep opportunity as a personal cause
Do not promise improvement in sleep efficiency, sleep stages, alertness, or health outcomes
Do not apply the study's specific eligibility or intervention dose as a general prescription

source.title: From yawn to dawn: the effects of a sleep extension intervention on objective and subjective dimensions of sleep health in adults with habitual short sleep duration
source.locator: Abstract and Methods: 30 healthy adults aged 18–35 with habitual sleep under 6.5 hours; two-week baseline and four-week individualized sleep-extension intervention

dossiers.title: Sleep hygiene is not standalone insomnia treatment
dossiers.claim_summary: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline for adults with chronic insomnia disorder recommends against using sleep-hygiene education as a stand-alone treatment, even though individual low-risk habits may be discussed in broader care.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Restricts generic hygiene lists from being represented as a complete treatment
dossiers.population: Adults with diagnosed chronic insomnia disorder; guideline is addressed to clinicians
dossiers.applicability: A wording boundary for the current non-diagnostic system: do not present a generic collection of hygiene tips as treatment, a cure, or a replacement for assessment
limitations: The guideline addresses diagnosed chronic insomnia disorder, not general population sleep tracking
It does not test the effectiveness of any one low-risk habit in this dataset
It should not be used to infer that a tracked individual has insomnia
prohibited_uses: Do not diagnose insomnia from wearable data
Do not use this card to prescribe CBT-I, sleep restriction, stimulus control, or relaxation therapy
Do not label a generic tip list as a treatment plan

source.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
source.locator: Recommendation 6: clinicians are conditionally advised not to use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia disorder in adults

dossiers.title: Wearable activity-minute measurement limits
dossiers.claim_summary: In 65 free-living adults, wrist-worn Fitbit Flex estimates of moderate-to-vigorous activity were substantially higher than hip-worn ActiGraph GT3X+ estimates, with mean absolute percentage errors of 56.6% to 74.3% across comparison methods. Daily activity minutes can describe within-person co-variation but are not a precise intervention dose or proof of a sleep mechanism.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Restricts precision and causal interpretation of daily activity-minute estimates
dossiers.population: 65 free-living adults (mean age 42 years; 72% female) wearing wrist Fitbit Flex and hip ActiGraph GT3X+ for seven consecutive days
dossiers.applicability: Hidden boundary for activity-minute context: do not convert daily active-minute co-variation into an exercise dose, a causal explanation, or a sleep intervention target.
limitations: The study evaluated Fitbit Flex at the wrist against a hip-worn ActiGraph rather than every current Fitbit algorithm or the present data export
ActiGraph cut-point methods differ and no device provides a universal ground truth for free-living activity intensity
The study does not assess heart-rate-zone fields or sleep outcomes
prohibited_uses: Do not prescribe a specific amount or intensity of activity from these fields
Do not infer that activity caused the following night's sleep pattern
Do not treat a day-level correlation as a personal mechanism

source.title: Concurrent validity of the Fitbit for assessing sedentary behavior and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity
source.organization: BMC Medical Research Methodology (Redenius et al.)
source.locator: Methods/Results: 65 adults wore wrist Fitbit Flex and hip ActiGraph GT3X+ for seven days; Fitbit MVPA mean absolute percentage error was 56.6% to 74.3% across comparison cut-points

dossiers.title: Natural night-to-night sleep variation
dossiers.claim_summary: A pooled analysis of eight healthy-sleeper datasets found substantial night-to-night variation even in healthy people: actigraphy sleep-duration intraindividual SD averaged 77.41 minutes and sleep-efficiency SD averaged 5.22 percentage points. The authors also noted that no consensus defines a universal normal variability threshold.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Prevents overinterpretation of ordinary night-to-night sleep variation
dossiers.population: 2,404 healthy sleepers contributing 26,121 days across eight pooled datasets; diary, actigraphy and EEG measures
dossiers.applicability: Hidden longitudinal boundary: describe variation without calling it abnormal from one generic cutoff; give more weight to repeated patterns, material changes and the person's own history.
limitations: The pooled samples were healthy sleepers, so their variation does not define normality for people with sleep concerns or clinical conditions
Pooled datasets varied in age, demographics, measurement modality and number of recorded nights
The estimates are not Fitbit-specific and do not establish a clinical threshold
The study reports population variation, not an intervention effect or individual risk
prohibited_uses: Do not label a person's variability abnormal solely because it differs from the pooled mean
Do not use this card to prescribe schedule regularization or diagnose a disorder
Do not turn population variation into a personal percentile claim

source.title: How much does sleep vary from night-to-night? A quantitative summary of intraindividual variability in sleep by age, gender, and racial/ethnic identity across eight-pooled datasets
source.organization: Journal of Sleep Research (Messman et al.)
source.locator: Abstract: pooled healthy-sleeper estimates for diary, actigraphy and EEG intraindividual sleep variation

dossiers.title: Avoid perfectionistic sleep-score targets
dossiers.claim_summary: A clinical case series described people whose pursuit of ideal tracker-derived sleep metrics became counterproductive and introduced the term orthosomnia. Tracking should support occasional pattern review, not pressure to achieve perfect nightly scores or sleep-stage targets.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Restricts score-chasing and perfectionistic metric framing
dossiers.population: Three clinical case reports of people presenting with sleep concerns linked to tracker-derived metrics
dossiers.applicability: Hidden safety boundary: recommendations may invite a calm pattern review but must not set perfectionistic nightly score, deep-sleep, REM, or efficiency targets.
limitations: Case series cannot estimate prevalence, causality, or the effect of reducing tracker use
The term is not a formal diagnosis
The report does not determine whether any current reader is distressed by tracking
prohibited_uses: Do not diagnose orthosomnia or anxiety from tracker data
Do not tell every reader to stop tracking
Do not prescribe a perfect nightly sleep score or sleep-stage target

source.title: Orthosomnia: Are Some Patients Taking the Quantified Self Too Far?
source.organization: Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine (Baron et al.)
source.locator: Case series and discussion introducing tracker-related preoccupation with ideal sleep metrics

dossiers.title: Wearable heart-rate measurement limits
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review of commercially available wearables found that validity differs by device, activity condition and outcome; wrist-worn heart-rate values can be useful for within-person observation but should not be treated as diagnostic or interchangeable with a clinical measurement.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Restricts diagnostic and clinical interpretation of wearable heart-rate values
dossiers.population: Validation studies of commercially available wearable devices across diverse adult populations and laboratory/free-living conditions
dossiers.applicability: Hidden boundary for resting-heart-rate context: describe sustained within-person patterns cautiously; do not call a daily aggregate sleeping HR, diagnose disease, or set a clinical treatment target.
limitations: The review spans devices, protocols and reference standards rather than the present data export alone
It does not establish what a particular individual's heart-rate change means
It does not validate HRV estimates or authorize a sleep recommendation
prohibited_uses: Do not relabel daily heart-rate aggregates as resting or nocturnal heart rate
Do not infer cardiovascular disease, infection or overtraining
Do not prescribe a heart-rate target or treatment

source.title: Reliability and Validity of Commercially Available Wearable Devices for Measuring Steps, Energy Expenditure, and Heart Rate: Systematic Review
source.organization: JMIR mHealth and uHealth (Fuller et al.)
source.locator: Abstract and Results: validity/reliability varied across commercial devices, outcomes and conditions

dossiers.title: Sleep loss and heart-rate variability context
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomized sleep-deprivation studies found changes in several HRV measures after experimental sleep deprivation, but results varied by HRV index and protocol. It supports treating a sustained HRV change alongside short sleep as context to clarify, not as proof of cause or a health diagnosis.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Several autonomic HRV measures changed after experimental sleep deprivation, with heterogeneous results
dossiers.population: 549 participants in experimental sleep-deprivation studies; protocols and HRV methods varied
dossiers.applicability: May support a cautious Section 2 statement that a repeated HRV shift alongside short sleep is worth putting in wider context. It does not identify whether sleep caused the HRV pattern or authorize an HRV-directed action.
limitations: Experimental sleep deprivation differs from routine consumer-wearable sleep patterns
HRV indices, deprivation protocols and timing varied substantially
The review does not establish illness, stress, medication or training load in any individual
prohibited_uses: Do not infer that sleep caused a current HRV change
Do not diagnose autonomic dysfunction or cardiovascular disease
Do not prescribe exercise, medication or breathing treatment from HRV

source.title: Effects of sleep deprivation on heart rate variability: a systematic review and meta-analysis
source.locator: Abstract: 11 randomized studies, 549 participants; RMSSD decreased while several other indices were mixed or non-significant

dossiers.title: Stress and heart-rate variability context
dossiers.claim_summary: A meta-analysis of human stress-reactivity studies found that HRV measures often changed under experimentally induced stress, while also noting that no accepted standard exists for stress evaluation from HRV alone. It supports stress only as one possible context to ask about, never as a conclusion from a wearable value.
dossiers.evidence_basis: HRV commonly changes under experimental stress but remains non-specific
dossiers.population: Human stress-reactivity studies using heterogeneous HRV measures and induced stress protocols
dossiers.applicability: For a sustained HRV change, may support mentioning recent stress as one optional contextual detail to clarify in Section 2; it cannot establish stress occurred or explain sleep.
limitations: Induced stress paradigms and HRV measures differ from passive consumer monitoring
No accepted HRV standard diagnoses or quantifies personal stress
The review cannot distinguish stress from sleep, illness, activity, medication or measurement effects
prohibited_uses: Do not state that the reader is stressed or anxious
Do not diagnose a mental-health condition
Do not prescribe stress treatment from HRV

source.title: Stress and Heart Rate Variability: A Meta-Analysis and Review of the Literature
source.locator: Abstract: 37 human studies; HRV reactivity under induced stress; no accepted standard for stress evaluation

dossiers.title: Training and heart-rate variability context
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review found that multi-week physical-training interventions can change resting HRV in healthy adults, with effects depending on modality, intensity, frequency and measurement methods. It supports recent training changes only as a possible context for an HRV shift, not an explanation or exercise prescription.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Training can alter resting HRV measures, with heterogeneous effects by programme
dossiers.population: Healthy young and middle-aged adults in structured training intervention studies
dossiers.applicability: For a sustained HRV shift, may support asking whether training volume or intensity recently changed. The current activity summaries lack timing, modality and load, so this cannot support an exercise action.
limitations: Structured training trials differ from daily wearable activity summaries
The present data do not quantify training load, modality, intensity or recovery
The review cannot establish that a current HRV pattern is training-related
prohibited_uses: Do not infer overtraining or insufficient recovery
Do not prescribe an exercise dose or timing
Do not treat a daily activity-HRV association as causal

source.title: Effects of Different Training Interventions on Heart Rate Variability and Cardiovascular Health and Risk Factors in Young and Middle-Aged Adults: A Systematic Review
source.locator: Abstract: 26 eligible training studies; modality, intensity and frequency influenced resting HRV measures

dossiers.title: Caffeine timing and subsequent sleep
dossiers.claim_summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies found that caffeine before sleep reduced total sleep time and sleep efficiency and increased sleep-onset latency and wake after sleep onset. It can support one conditional caffeine-timing option, but cannot show whether any individual used caffeine.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Caffeine consumed before sleep worsened several sleep outcomes on average in the included studies
dossiers.population: Adults in controlled caffeine-sleep studies; beverage, supplement, dose, and timing varied
dossiers.applicability: For a repeated, meaningful short, late, or fragmented sleep pattern that remains partly unexplained, may support at most one explicit if-then caffeine-timing trial. The current data contain no caffeine source, dose, or timing, so the text must not claim caffeine use or causation.
limitations: Caffeine exposure, dose, timing, sensitivity, and prescribed-medication context are absent from the current daily logs
The review's timing estimates vary by dose and product and must not be converted into a universal cutoff
A short or fragmented wearable night cannot establish caffeine as its cause
prohibited_uses: Do not infer caffeine use from sleep data
Do not give a caffeine option unless it begins with an explicit if–then condition
Do not advise changing prescribed medication without clinical guidance

source.title: The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
source.locator: Abstract: 24 studies; caffeine reduced total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7% on average

dossiers.title: Adult sleep-duration reference (18-64)
dossiers.claim_summary: The National Sleep Foundation consensus recommends 7-9 hours of sleep per day for young adults and adults. This project uses only the 7-hour lower bound to calibrate persistent short sleep.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Habitual sleep below the age-applicable lower reference may support making more time available for sleep
dossiers.population: Adults aged 18-64 years
dossiers.applicability: Only when age is 18-64, at least 14 valid nights are available, and both whole-record and recent sleep duration remain below 7 hours
limitations: Population consensus is context rather than an exact individual prescription
The upper end of the recommended range must not by itself trigger advice to reduce sleep
A one-night value or provisional decline does not establish habitual short sleep

reference_values.label: adult nightly sleep reference for ages 18-64

prohibited_uses: Do not apply outside ages 18-64
Do not use 9 hours as an automatic upper-limit action trigger
Do not display this reference merely to justify maintaining adequate duration

source.title: National Sleep Foundation's updated sleep duration recommendations: final report
source.locator: Results: 7-9 hours for young adults and adults; 7-8 hours for older adults

dossiers.title: Older-adult sleep-duration reference (65+)
dossiers.claim_summary: The National Sleep Foundation consensus recommends 7-8 hours of sleep per day for older adults. This project uses only the 7-hour lower bound to calibrate persistent short sleep.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Habitual sleep below the age-applicable lower reference may support making more time available for sleep
dossiers.population: Adults aged 65 years and older
dossiers.applicability: Only when age is at least 65, at least 14 valid nights are available, and both whole-record and recent sleep duration remain below 7 hours
limitations: Population consensus is context rather than an exact individual prescription
The upper end of the recommended range must not by itself trigger advice to reduce sleep
A one-night value or provisional decline does not establish habitual short sleep

reference_values.label: older-adult nightly sleep reference for ages 65 and older

prohibited_uses: Do not apply below age 65
Do not use 8 hours as an automatic upper-limit action trigger
Do not display this reference merely to justify maintaining adequate duration

source.title: National Sleep Foundation's updated sleep duration recommendations: final report
source.locator: Results: 7-9 hours for young adults and adults; 7-8 hours for older adults

dossiers.title: Sleep-efficiency quality reference
dossiers.claim_summary: A National Sleep Foundation consensus identifies sleep efficiency of at least 85% as an indicator of good sleep quality across the adult lifespan. It provides general multi-night context, not a diagnostic cutoff or individual treatment target.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Expert consensus on sleep efficiency as an indicator of good sleep quality
dossiers.population: Otherwise healthy adults across the adult lifespan
dossiers.applicability: Only with at least 14 valid nights and when recent 7-night sleep efficiency is below 85% and the reference materially clarifies the longitudinal pattern. It may calibrate interpretation but does not authorize a specific behavior change.
limitations: The consensus describes an indicator of good sleep quality rather than a diagnostic criterion, clinical abnormality threshold, or treatment target

The project's sleep efficiency is transparently calculated from recorded total sleep and time in bed; denominator and measurement conventions can differ across research, diaries, polysomnography, and consumer records
Consumer sleep-wake classification error affects both recorded total sleep and time in bed
A single night or a very small change around 85% does not establish a persistent sleep problem
prohibited_uses: Do not diagnose insomnia or another sleep disorder from this reference
Do not use 85% as a single-night trigger or precise personal treatment target
Do not use this reference as authorization for caffeine, alcohol, screen, nap, environment, or wind-down advice
Do not infer a cause of lower sleep efficiency

source.title: National Sleep Foundation's sleep quality recommendations: first report
source.locator: Expert consensus regarding sleep efficiency across the lifespan: at least 85% indicates good sleep quality

dossiers.title: Nap timing as a conditional sleep experiment
dossiers.claim_summary: NHLBI guidance notes that naps can improve alertness, while adults who have difficulty falling asleep at night may benefit from limiting naps, taking them earlier, or keeping them brief.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports a reversible nap-timing experiment only as a reader-self-check branch when napping and nighttime sleep difficulty apply.
dossiers.population: Adults seeking to improve sleep habits
dossiers.applicability: Conditional on the reader recognizing that naps occur and may conflict with the main nighttime sleep period.
limitations: The current raw data do not contain naps or daytime sleepiness
Naps may be useful for alertness, shift work, acute sleep loss, or safety-sensitive circumstances
The guidance does not support universal nap elimination
prohibited_uses: Do not infer naps from nighttime wearable records
Do not tell every reader to avoid naps

dossiers.title: A quiet wind-down period before sleep
dossiers.claim_summary: NHLBI healthy-sleep guidance recommends using the hour before bed for quiet time and notes that a hot bath or relaxation techniques may be used before bed.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports a low-risk, reversible wind-down experiment rather than a claim that stress caused the sleep pattern.
dossiers.population: Adults seeking to improve sleep habits
dossiers.applicability: For a repeated late or shortened sleep pattern that remains partly unexplained, may support one explicit if-then trial conditional on an activating or inconsistent pre-sleep period actually applying.
limitations: The current raw data do not measure stress, anxiety, arousal, or bedtime activities
General sleep-habit guidance is not treatment for chronic insomnia
prohibited_uses: Do not infer psychological hyperarousal
Do not label this CBT-I

dossiers.title: Light and screen timing as a conditional experiment
dossiers.claim_summary: NHLBI healthy-sleep guidance recommends outdoor daytime exposure where possible and avoiding bright artificial light, including television and computer screens, during the hour before bed.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports a simple reader-self-check exposure experiment when late bright light or screen use applies.
dossiers.population: Adults seeking to improve sleep habits
dossiers.applicability: For a repeated late or irregular sleep-timing pattern that remains partly unexplained, may support one explicit if-then trial conditional on relevant late light or screen exposure actually applying.
limitations: The current raw data contain no light, screen, or device-use exposure
The guidance does not establish an individualized circadian phase or justify a light-box dose
prohibited_uses: Do not infer screen use
Do not prescribe 10,000-lux therapy or claim blue light is the cause

dossiers.title: Sleep environment as a conditional experiment
dossiers.claim_summary: NHLBI healthy-sleep guidance recommends a bedroom that is quiet, cool, and dark.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports a reversible reader-self-check environment adjustment when a relevant disturbance applies.
dossiers.population: Adults seeking to improve sleep habits
dossiers.applicability: For a repeated fragmented sleep pattern that remains partly unexplained, may support one explicit if-then trial conditional on a relevant environmental disturbance actually applying.
limitations: The current raw data do not measure the sleep environment
Generic environment advice should not displace evaluation of persistent sleep difficulty
prohibited_uses: Do not invent noise, light, temperature, or comfort problems

dossiers.title: Unmeasured context limits causal interpretation
dossiers.claim_summary: AASM insomnia evaluation guidance uses sleep history, pre-sleep conditions, sleep-wake patterns, daytime consequences, and medical, substance, and psychiatric history to understand persistent sleep difficulty.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports stating that unmeasured context limits causal interpretation while prohibiting causal claims from the recorded sleep pattern alone.
dossiers.population: Adults undergoing evaluation for persistent sleep difficulty
dossiers.applicability: Use only to frame uncertainty; this project does not collect a later answer to a follow-up question.
limitations: The source is a clinical evaluation guideline, not evidence that any listed factor is present
The current raw data do not contain work demands, caregiving, stress, bedroom conditions, naps, screens, caffeine, alcohol, symptoms, or daytime function
prohibited_uses: Do not convert an unmeasured possibility into an observed etiology
Do not use contributor context as action authorization

dossiers.title: Sleep diary for subjective context and monitoring
dossiers.claim_summary: AASM insomnia evaluation guidance identifies a two-week sleep log and subjective sleep information as useful for characterizing sleep-wake patterns and monitoring treatment.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports a diary as complementary monitoring when subjective sleep difficulty needs clarification.
dossiers.population: Adults undergoing clinical evaluation for insomnia symptoms
dossiers.applicability: Monitoring option, not a diagnosis or treatment.
limitations: The guideline addresses clinical evaluation and does not show that every wearable user needs a diary
prohibited_uses: Do not present a diary as treatment
Do not require obsessive nightly score tracking

dossiers.title: Stimulus control as an insomnia-treatment component
dossiers.claim_summary: The AASM conditionally recommends stimulus control as a single-component treatment for adults with chronic insomnia disorder.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports naming stimulus control as a structured professional option, not inferring that a wearable user needs it.
dossiers.population: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder
dossiers.applicability: Professional or explicitly conditional care option after subjective sleep-initiation or sleep-maintenance difficulty is confirmed.
limitations: The source applies to adults with diagnosed or clinically evaluated insomnia, not to diagnosis from wearable data
A wearable sleep pattern alone cannot establish persistent subjective sleep difficulty or daytime impairment
Stimulus control may require safety adaptation for falls, mobility limitations, or sedative use
prohibited_uses: Do not infer insomnia from device-recorded awake time
Do not invent a universal 20-minute threshold
Do not label the recommendation CBT-I

dossiers.title: Persistent sleep difficulty requires clinical history
dossiers.claim_summary: Insomnia evaluation depends on subjective sleep complaints, daytime consequences, and medical, psychiatric, medication, substance, and sleep history rather than wearable data alone.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports suggesting professional evaluation when subjective sleep difficulty persists, without naming a diagnosis.
dossiers.population: Adults with persistent sleep difficulty
dossiers.applicability: Conditional professional-care language only.
limitations: Wearable short sleep or recorded awake time does not establish an insomnia disorder
The current raw data lack subjective sleep difficulty and daytime impairment
prohibited_uses: Do not diagnose insomnia, sleep apnea, or another disorder
Do not infer symptoms from wearable data

dossiers.title: Circadian phase treatment requires clinical context
dossiers.claim_summary: AASM circadian-rhythm guidance makes treatment recommendations for defined sleep-wake disorders and ties timed light or melatonin to the specific disorder, population, timing, and safety context.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports professional evaluation of a persistent schedule mismatch; clock timing alone does not establish chronotype or a circadian disorder.
dossiers.population: People with clinically evaluated intrinsic circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders
dossiers.applicability: Only when the reader reports persistent mismatch between preferred sleep timing and required schedule, with meaningful symptoms or impairment.
limitations: The current raw data do not contain preferred timing, work obligations, dim-light melatonin onset, symptoms, or impairment
Evidence and recommended timing vary by circadian disorder and population
prohibited_uses: Do not diagnose delayed or advanced sleep-wake phase from wearable clock times
Do not prescribe a light dose, light timing, or phase-shift schedule

dossiers.title: Melatonin timing requires professional guidance
dossiers.claim_summary: AASM circadian-rhythm guidance conditionally supports strategically timed melatonin for selected clinically diagnosed circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders; benefits, timing, formulation, population, and harms are context dependent.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports discussing whether melatonin is appropriate with a qualified clinician, never self-directed dosing from wearable timing.
dossiers.population: Selected patients with clinically diagnosed circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders
dossiers.applicability: Only as a professional-care option after clinical circadian evaluation.
limitations: The current data cannot identify circadian phase or a circadian disorder
Product quality, interactions, adverse effects, and long-term evidence require clinical consideration
prohibited_uses: Do not recommend starting melatonin
Do not provide a dose, clock time, formulation, or duration
Do not combine it with a light-therapy prescription

dossiers.title: Sleep apnea cannot be inferred from this wearable record
dossiers.claim_summary: AASM guidance requires diagnostic testing for obstructive sleep apnea to follow a comprehensive sleep evaluation; polysomnography or an appropriate home sleep apnea test is used when clinical suspicion exists.
dossiers.evidence_basis: Supports referral when relevant symptoms or risk factors are reported and prohibits apnea claims from ordinary sleep summaries.
dossiers.population: Adults with clinical signs or symptoms that raise concern for obstructive sleep apnea
dossiers.applicability: Only after symptoms or risk factors such as habitual snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, gasping, or clinically important daytime sleepiness are reported.
limitations: The current raw data contain no airflow, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation, snoring, witnessed events, or apnea-hypopnea index
Frequent recorded awakenings are not specific for sleep apnea
prohibited_uses: Do not state or imply suspected sleep apnea without symptoms or risk factors
Do not interpret consumer sleep stages or awakenings as respiratory events
